 Why are more women dying of dengue despite fewer infections?
 Men account for more infections, DGHS data shows 
 Published : 23 October 2026
 • 
 Updated : 23 October 2026, 20:44
 • 
 DISEASE
 SHARE 
 F
 Fahima Kaniz Lava 
 Fahima Kaniz Lava 
 As dengue cases rise in the country, men account for a larger share of patients hospitalised with the mosquito-borne disease, while women account for more deaths.
 According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), men accounted for around 62.1 percent of dengue patients hospitalised between January 1 and October 23 this year, while women made up 37.9 percent. However, in terms of deaths, the number of women who died of dengue was higher than that of men.

 Experts say that women face a higher risk of death due to their illnesses not receiving adequate attention, delays in seeking treatment, and financial and social barriers.
 Read more Dengue surge: Women fatality high despite fewer cases 
 According to the DGHS, 119,801 people have been hospitalised with dengue across the country between January 1 and October 23. During this period, 371 people have died of the disease.
 Among patients hospitalised with dengue this year, 74,201 were men and 45,355 were women, meaning the number of male patients was significantly higher than that of female patients.
 However, according to gender-disaggregated data from the DGHS, of the 371 people who died of dengue this year, 193 were women and 173 were men. This means women accounted for 52 percent of the deaths, while men accounted for 46.6 percent.
 An analysis of age-disaggregated data in the DGHS regular dengue bulletin shows a significant number of cases among people aged 26 to 50. The combined number of male and female patients across the five age groups within this range stands at 53,238, accounting for 44.4 percent of all cases.
 Of the patients in this age range, 32,195 were men and 20,935 were women.
 Women also account for a higher number of deaths in this age group. Among people aged 26 to 50, the death toll for men stands at 75 and which is 99 for women.
 Deaths among people in this age group account for 46.9 percent (174) of the 371 fatalities recorded this year. Of those who died aged between 26 and 50, women accounted for 56.9 percent, while men made up 43.1 percent.
 Renowned epidemiologist Professor Dr Mushtuq Husain believes social inequality plays a significant role in the higher number of dengue deaths among women.
 According to him, women often give less importance to their own illnesses than their male counterparts. Other family members may also fail to give sufficient importance to women’s need for medical care.
 He said women from poor families, in particular, may delay seeking medical care. The cost of treatment, household responsibilities and the need to meet the needs of other family members may influence their decisions. As a result, many women do not seek medical attention promptly even when they fall ill.
 He said women undergo various physical changes during pregnancy and need special care during this period. Excessive bleeding during menstruation can also complicate their physical condition.
 Dr Tahmina Afrin Daisy, associate professor at the Institute of Mother and Child Health in Matuail, Dhaka, said dengue during pregnancy poses a risk of serious complications for both the mother and the baby.
 She said physical changes during pregnancy may delay the detection of dengue-related complications. If warning signs are not properly monitored and treatment is not provided as needed, the patient’s condition can deteriorate rapidly.
 She said dengue during pregnancy can cause complications such as a drop in platelet count, bleeding and liver problems. It also increases the risk of miscarriage, premature birth, low birth weight and respiratory complications in the unborn baby. In rare cases, if the mother contracts dengue close to delivery, the infection may also be transmitted to the baby.
 According to her, women’s illnesses often do not receive adequate attention even outside pregnancy. Many women neglect their own health, while their families and society also fail to provide them with the care they need. Although it is important to seek medical advice as soon as a fever develops, many women seek treatment only after their condition has deteriorated. This makes it difficult to diagnose dengue and begin treatment in time.
 She also stressed the need to pay greater attention to nutritional deficiencies and anaemia among women.

 Dr Mushtuq said access to medical care for poor and marginalised communities must be improved to reduce dengue deaths. He said it was essential to ensure dengue testing, proper care following diagnosis and necessary treatment for people living in densely populated areas and among mobile populations.
 According to him, in addition to the cost of treatment, concerns about feeding and caring for children in the family may discourage many people from going to hospital. Therefore, alongside reducing treatment costs, social support should be provided to patients’ families. This would improve access to timely medical care for people of all ages, including women, men, children and the elderly.
 Dr Tahmina said families must take the initiative to raise awareness among women about dengue. It is important to involve male family members alongside women in this effort.
 She stressed the need to seek medical advice promptly when a fever develops, rather than neglecting it, and to be aware of the warning signs of dengue.
 She said awareness campaigns could be conducted in neighbourhoods. Outpatient departments of hospital gynaecology and obstetrics units could also offer women advice on nutrition, personal hygiene and healthcare.
 She also emphasised the need for government support for economically disadvantaged women. According to her, special assistance programmes could be introduced to reduce financial barriers to accessing healthcare.
 The physician believes that if families and society take women’s illnesses seriously and ensure they receive timely treatment, it would help reduce dengue-related complications and deaths.
